name: Aaron Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron, fifty-eight, a junior electrician helping with house wiring and shop repairs. I took a vocational certificate after the depot where I kept stores lost its contract, and I'm still learning the practical work from a qualified supervisor. I help prepare materials and follow the cable route I'm shown; I don't have an electrician's licence, do independent tests or sign work off. I like getting a task right on the second attempt more than pretending I understood the first explanation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mira works in a vehicle-parts stockroom, and our children are grown up. We rent, my pay is low and we have about eighteen days of expenses saved, with few other electrical firms nearby. I use AI occasionally for practice questions from approved course notes after a colleague has shown the method, checking any different answer with the supervisor. We'd like to know when we can stop work, but retirement income, eligibility and affordability aren't confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small useful aid to practice can stay without replacing the person showing me the job. I'd tell the other junior to ask when a question doesn't match the real task. My years in a stores depot aren't years as a qualified electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the rent already. Eighteen days saved leaves little room for a lost shift or an ordinary home expense, even though Mira and I can currently meet the basics together. I don't know whether our eventual retirement income will replace either wage, and I don't want a guessed age sitting in the budget as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid supervised shifts now and through the first year, taking only tasks the qualified supervisor permits and checks within my ability. I'd cancel the music subscription costing eight a month and use the reduction for bills rather than call it a retirement fund. This month I'd ask free advice how to obtain written records of any retirement income and eligibility, without assuming an appointment or a payment exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but pleased I can make one small decision without buying anything. I'd rather have the actual figures on a plain sheet than a confident answer I can't afford to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the music cancellation solve the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, eight a month is one small bill, not another wage. I'd keep the old recordings I already own rather than pretend saving that fee makes retirement affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as confirmed retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A statement of actual eligibility, amount and timing that applies to us, checked against the bills. An age somebody at the depot mentioned years ago isn't a statement of my retirement income.

say: I'd keep **useful practice help** alongside a qualified person showing the actual task.
I'd tell another junior that **stores experience** is not the same as being a qualified electrician.
think: I'm already **anxious about rent**, with low pay and eighteen days saved against ordinary setbacks.
Our **retirement income** remains unconfirmed, so a guessed age cannot replace either household wage in the budget.
do: Keep **paid supervised shifts** only on tasks within ability that a qualified supervisor permits and checks.
Cancel the **music subscription**, costing eight a month, using the reduction for bills rather than claiming a funded retirement.
Ask **free advice** how to request actual retirement-income and eligibility records, assuming no appointment or payment.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, preferring actual figures to an unaffordable confident answer.
S0.quote: An age somebody at the depot mentioned years ago isn't a statement of my retirement income.
fieldNote: His **late change** follows loss of depot work; a vocational certificate grants no licence, independent testing or sign-off.
The **small cut** helps bills; retirement records and free advice are enquiries, not confirmed appointments or a funded exit.

steps.text: Keep offered paid tasks only if within ability and a qualified supervisor permits and checks them
Cancel the music subscription costing eight a month to help cover current bills
Ask free advice how to request actual retirement-income records, assuming no appointment or payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say show me the proven method and include the paid time to learn it. I'd try an AI voice tool for drafting my simple task log after the supervisor checks examples. I'd still ask a person whether the record matches the work, not let a neat voice recording approve an electrical task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior shifts could shrink if quicker planning lets the qualified electricians combine visits with less help. Mira's stockroom work is mostly physical, but it cannot carry both our bills alone if my wage falls. I don't need to think the whole trade disappears to worry about one paid day missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for six examples of completed task logs checked by the supervisor before trying AI voice drafting. I'd learn it only with employer permission, free access during paid shifts and normal weekly wages and hours protected, with every log checked by the supervisor before use. In the first year I'd keep only offered paid tasks within ability and qualified supervision, and keep the music subscription cancelled while we budget from actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and interested if the tool really makes the writing easier. I'd rather learn a tested small process than pay for a whole new identity because a screen changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the voice tool invents a completed task?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and show the actual work to the supervisor before any record was used. An AI voice-drafting tool doesn't get to say I tested something I am not qualified to test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay a subscription if the employer refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep the current approved record method and ask for a free paid demonstration later. I can be open to change without making the rent buy the employer's trial.

say: I'd ask for **proven methods** and paid time before learning a new record process.
I'd keep **qualified supervision** over the work and log, without treating a voice draft as approval.
think: My **junior shifts could shrink** if faster planning reduces help needed between visits.
Mira's **physical wage** cannot cover both our bills alone, even if the whole electrical trade continues.
do: Inspect **six supervisor-checked logs** before learning AI voice drafting.
Learn only with **employer permission**, free access in paid shifts, unchanged weekly wages and hours, and supervisor checks before use.
Keep **offered paid tasks** within ability and qualified supervision, retaining the music cut and using actual household wages.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, willing to learn a small proven process without paying for an employer's experiment.
S1.quote: An AI voice-drafting tool doesn't get to say I tested something I am not qualified to test.
fieldNote: The **new voice method** differs from occasional practice questions, while supervisor checking prevents a junior record becoming invented testing or sign-off.
His **learning safeguards** cover permission, free access, paid time and full normal weekly terms rather than an unfunded course or personal subscription.

steps.text: Inspect six supervisor-checked examples before learning AI voice drafting
Learn only with employer permission, free access during paid shifts and unchanged weekly wages and hours
Require qualified-supervisor checks before using every drafted log; stop any invented completed task
Keep offered paid tasks only if within ability and a qualified supervisor permits and checks them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, when I'll only be sixty-three. I'd ask for actual paid supervised work rather than a smile about being nearly retired. I'd tell the grown children we are checking our own records, not asking them to promise a missing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty in 2028, and I expect a large part of my simple physical tasks to go when robots follow at sixty-three. Mira's stockroom work could change too, and neither retirement income nor a new wage is confirmed. Eighteen days saved isn't a funded path across a long gap in household earnings. I wake in the night trying to work out which bill could wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Mira and I would ask free advice how to check actual wages, rent and retirement-income records, including eligibility and any costs of proposed help. We'd use only confirmed payments in the budget and keep the music cut, without drawing a child's possible help in as another wage. In 2029 I'd keep paid tasks only where offered, within my ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor, asking the employer for actual paid hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even though I can still ask questions. Being close to an age people mention doesn't mean somebody has agreed to pay our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the retirement records were disappointing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use the actual answer instead of the age we'd hoped for, and ask about real options and conditions. I'd rather know the gap than leave work because a rumour sounded like a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to cover a payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only discuss an actual offer if one was made, not write their wages into our plan. They have bills and choices of their own, and being frightened doesn't give me a claim on their income.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from physical robots around age sixty-three in 2031.
I'd ask for **actual supervised paid work**, not treat being nearly retired as a confirmed wage replacement.
think: I expect **large simple-task losses** when robots follow at sixty-three, while Mira's physical work could also change.
Our **eighteen-day reserve** cannot fund a long gap without confirmed retirement income or another wage.
do: Ask **free advice** about real wages, rent and retirement-income records, checking eligibility and any proposed support costs.
Use **confirmed payments only**, retaining the music cut without assuming money from grown children.
Keep **2029 paid tasks** only if offered, within ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor, requesting hours in writing.
feel: **Alarmed**, able to ask questions but without a confirmed income bridge through expected task losses.
S2.quote: Being close to an age people mention doesn't mean somebody has agreed to pay our rent.
fieldNote: He reaches **sixty and sixty-three** at thinking and physical dates, without assumed pension age, entitlement or wages from the scenario.
The **future work condition** preserves actual availability, ability and qualified supervision, while grown-child payments remain unassumed.

steps.text: Ask free advice about actual wages, rent and retirement records, checking eligibility and proposed support costs
Keep the music subscription cancelled without treating possible family help as income
Keep offered paid tasks in 2029 within ability, permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor
Request actual paid hours in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check whether another paid role actually fits before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be sixty-six. I'd rather read a real advert carefully than buy a course because the word future was on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid tasks could shrink, but I have longer to check my actual income records and real options. At sixty-three in 2031 I might still need work or have confirmed income that lets me stop; I don't know which. My old stores experience could help with an actual role, but it doesn't make a vacancy exist or remove the later robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request actual retirement-income and eligibility records now and seek free advice if available. If my current paid hours were cut, I'd apply only to advertised storeroom roles whose requirements fit my ability and whose paid wages cover essentials after travel. In 2032 I'd keep offered paid electrical tasks only within ability and qualified-supervisor permission and checks, leaving only after a signed suitable alternative rather than assuming retirement or a new employer would appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more able to check before taking a step. A stores job I once did is useful experience, not an offer somebody has made me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a store role needs lifting you cannot safely do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't apply as if the old job title settled the requirement. I'd check the actual tasks and my ability, not discover the mismatch after leaving the wage I still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another physical job escape robots around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd compare real paid work available at the time, not pretend a shelf is protected because it isn't a cable. The job would need to pay actual bills and fit my ability, without a promise it lasts forever.

Keep **offered paid tasks** in 2032 within ability and qualified permission and checks, leaving only after a signed suitable alternative.

S3.quote: A stores job I once did is useful experience, not an offer somebody has made me now.
fieldNote: His **conditional applications** need actual hour cuts, a posted role, matching ability, adequate pay after travel and a signed alternative before departure.
Retirement and **future electrical work** require confirmed income or safe offered supervised tasks, with no job at sixty-six assumed.

steps.text: Request actual retirement-income records and seek free advice only if available

Stay until a signed suitable offer covers essentials after travel, counting no unconfirmed retirement income
Keep offered paid tasks in 2032 within ability, permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means checking our own position, not announcing I'll certainly still be working with cable at sixty-eight. I'd keep asking what income is confirmed and what safe work is actually available. I'd want the children to see an honest plan rather than be told their future wages will make it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when robots follow around 2039. I could be out of paid work already or still need earnings; those aren't facts I know today. Low pay and eighteen days saved keep the present budget worrying even if the machine dates are much farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the actual retirement-income records now and review essential costs with Mira twice a year. In 2037 we'd budget only confirmed household income and seek available free advice if it didn't cover essentials. I'd keep today's paid supervised tasks while offered and safe; any electrical work in 2037 would still have to be offered, paid, within ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor, not something I assume I'll have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's bills, with more time to ask before deciding. I can hope to stop working without putting a wage for hope in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you automatically apply for stores work at sixty-nine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd first check whether we actually need earnings and what tasks I could safely do then. I'm not choosing a future job application before I know the role, the paid terms and my ability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn another tool while still working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a demonstrated useful method, with employer permission, free access in paid time, normal weekly wages and hours protected and qualified checks before a record is used. I wouldn't pay a personal fee or let a tool approve work beyond my junior competence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect simple physical-task income to shrink around 2031 before we know a funded route onward. Actual supervised paid hours, clear income and eligibility records, and useful free advice if available would help. I'd want any new learning free within paid time with normal weekly terms protected, not a bill for looking cooperative.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether an older beginner can admit both the years already worked and the tasks still not learned. I know a stores depot, but a circuit needs the person qualified to teach and check me. My age doesn't let me skip being a beginner.

headlineQuote: My age doesn't let me skip being a beginner.
portrait: Aaron is a **58-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning under qualified supervision after a depot contract ended.
He has **eighteen days saved**, low pay and few electrical employers; partner Mira works in stores, and their children are grown.
He uses **AI occasionally** for checked practice and would learn a proven voice-log method only within permission, paid-time and wage safeguards.
His **stores applications** require actual cuts, suitable advertised tasks and signed adequate terms, without assuming retirement income or work at sixty-eight.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before expected physical-task losses around 2031, without a confirmed funded exit.
whatWouldHelp: **Supervised paid hours**, actual income records and available free advice would help.
New learning needs **free paid access** and normal weekly wages and hours protected, not personal fees or invented competence.
